claim: Interferon-lambda (IFN-λ) protects intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) from enteric viruses by inducing expression of antiviral IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs).
source: Interferon-lambda (IFN-λ) protects intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) from enteric viruses by inducing expression of antiviral IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about IFN-λ function.

claim: Bacterial microbiota stimulate a homeostatic ISG signature in the intestine of specific pathogen-free mice.
source: Here, we find that bacterial microbiota stimulate a homeostatic ISG signature in the intestine of specific pathogen-free mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Homeostatic ISG expression is restricted to IECs.
source: This homeostatic ISG expression is restricted to IECs
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing ISG expression in epithelial fractions but not lamina propria (Figure 4A).

claim: Homeostatic ISG expression depends on IEC-intrinsic expression of IFN-λ receptor (Ifnlr1).
source: This homeostatic ISG expression is restricted to IECs, depends on IEC-intrinsic expression of IFN-λ receptor (Ifnlr1)
evidence: This is supported by data from conditional knockout mice (Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO) showing loss of ISG expression (Figures 4B-C, 6E-G).

claim: Homeostatic ISG expression is associated with IFN-λ production by leukocytes.
source: This homeostatic ISG expression is restricted to IECs, depends on IEC-intrinsic expression of IFN-λ receptor (Ifnlr1), and is associated with IFN-λ production by leukocytes.
evidence: This is supported by data showing Ifnl2/3 expression in CD45+ cells (Figure 5A).

claim: Homeostatic ISGs localize to pockets of the epithelium.
source: Strikingly, imaging of these homeostatic ISGs reveals localization to pockets of the epithelium
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope imaging data showing localized Ifit1 expression (Figure 6).

claim: Homeostatic ISGs are concentrated in mature IECs.
source: imaging of these homeostatic ISGs reveals localization to pockets of the epithelium and concentration in mature IECs.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing ISG expression toward villus tips (Figure 6A) and single-cell RNA-seq analysis (Figure 7).

claim: A minority of mature IECs express homeostatic ISGs in public single-cell RNA sequencing datasets from mice and humans.
source: Correspondingly, a minority of mature IECs express these ISGs in public single-cell RNA sequencing datasets from mice and humans.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of scRNA-seq datasets showing <20% of enterocytes express ISGs (Figure 7).

claim: Orally administered bacterial components can restore localized ISGs in mice lacking bacterial microbiota.
source: Furthermore, we assessed the ability of orally administered bacterial components to restore localized ISGs in mice lacking bacterial microbiota.
evidence: This is supported by data showing LPS and fecal transplant can restore Ifit1 expression in ABX-treated mice (Figure 8).

claim: IECs lacking Ifnlr1 are hyper-susceptible to initiation of murine rotavirus infection.
source: Lastly, we find that IECs lacking Ifnlr1 are hyper-susceptible to initiation of murine rotavirus infection.
evidence: This is supported by data showing increased mRV infection in Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO mice at early timepoints (Figure 9).

claim: Bacterial microbiota stimulate ISGs in localized regions of the intestinal epithelium at homeostasis, thereby preemptively activating antiviral defenses in vulnerable IECs to improve host defense against enteric viruses.
source: These observations indicate that bacterial microbiota stimulate ISGs in localized regions of the intestinal epithelium at homeostasis, thereby preemptively activating antiviral defenses in vulnerable IECs to improve host defense against enteric viruses.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence throughout the manuscript.

claim: Type I IFNs are directly stimulated by host detection of microbe-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs) such as viral nucleic acids.
source: Type I and III IFNs are directly stimulated by host detection of microbe-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs) such as viral nucleic acids
evidence: This is established knowledge about IFN induction mechanisms.

claim: Type III IFNs are directly stimulated by host detection of microbe-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs) such as viral nucleic acids.
source: Type I and III IFNs are directly stimulated by host detection of microbe-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs) such as viral nucleic acids
evidence: This is established knowledge about IFN induction mechanisms.

claim: The type I IFN receptor is expressed broadly across most cell types.
source: The type I IFN receptor is expressed broadly across most cell types, whereas the type III IFN receptor, Ifnlr1, is primarily restricted to epithelial cells (Kotenko and Durbin, 2017; Sommereyns et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The type III IFN receptor, Ifnlr1, is primarily restricted to epithelial cells.
source: The type I IFN receptor is expressed broadly across most cell types, whereas the type III IFN receptor, Ifnlr1, is primarily restricted to epithelial cells (Kotenko and Durbin, 2017; Sommereyns et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IFN-λ is of particular importance in effective antiviral defense of barrier tissues.
source: Accordingly, IFN-λ is of particular importance in effective antiviral defense of barrier tissues.
evidence: This is inferred from the restricted expression of Ifnlr1 to epithelial cells.

claim: Intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) are hyporesponsive to type I IFN in mice.
source: Interestingly, previous studies in mice have noted that intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) are hyporesponsive to type I IFN (Lin et al., 2016; Hernández et al., 2015; Pott et al., 2011; Van Winkle et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: The responsiveness of IECs to type I IFN is developmentally regulated because the IECs of adult mice exhibit weaker type I responses than IECs of neonatal mice.
source: The responsiveness of IECs to type I IFN appears to be developmentally regulated because the IECs of adult mice exhibit weaker type I responses than IECs of neonatal mice (Lin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: IFN-λ is the predominant antiviral IFN type that controls viral replication in the gastrointestinal epithelium.
source: Additionally, infection of mice deficient in IFN receptors (Ifnar1, Ifngr1, Ifnlr1; single or double knockouts) with enteric viruses indicates that IFN-λ is the predominant antiviral IFN type that controls viral replication in the gastrointestinal epithelium (Hernández et al., 2015; Nice et al., 2015; Pott et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies using knockout mice.

claim: IECs can robustly respond to IFN-λ with upregulation of canonical antiviral ISGs and increased resistance to infection by enteric viruses, such as rotaviruses and noroviruses.
source: IECs can robustly respond to IFN-λ with upregulation of canonical antiviral ISGs and increased resistance to infection by enteric viruses, such as rotaviruses and noroviruses (Baldridge et al., 2017; Nice et al., 2015; Pott et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mouse rotavirus is a natural pathogen of mice that infects enterocytes located at the tips of villi in the small intestine.
source: Mouse rotavirus is a natural pathogen of mice that infects enterocytes located at the tips of villi in the small intestine (Burns et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Rotaviruses have developed mechanisms to antagonize the induction of IFN by infected cells.
source: Rotaviruses have developed mechanisms to antagonize the induction of IFN by infected cells, suggesting that evasion of the IFN response is necessary for efficient epithelial infection (Arnold et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Prophylactic administration of IFN-λ significantly reduces the burden of mRV infection.
source: Indeed, prophylactic administration of IFN-λ significantly reduces the burden of mRV infection, demonstrating its potential for mediating epithelial antiviral immunity to this pathogen (Mahlakõiv et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2016; Pott et al., 2011; Van Winkle et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The bacterial microbiota in the intestine perform critical functions by aiding in host metabolism.
source: The bacterial microbiota in the intestine perform critical functions by aiding in host metabolism (Krajmalnik-Brown et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The bacterial microbiota in the intestine provide a competitive environment to defend against pathogens.
source: The bacterial microbiota in the intestine perform critical functions by aiding in host metabolism (Krajmalnik-Brown et al., 2012), providing a competitive environment to defend against pathogens (Kim et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The bacterial microbiota in the intestine initiate and maintain host immune function during homeostasis.
source: The bacterial microbiota in the intestine perform critical functions by aiding in host metabolism (Krajmalnik-Brown et al., 2012), providing a competitive environment to defend against pathogens (Kim et al., 2017), and initiating and maintaining host immune function during homeostasis (Honda and Littman, 2016; Rooks and Garrett, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Signals from the bacterial microbiota elicit a steady-state type I IFN response in systemic tissues and cell types that can prime antiviral immunity.
source: Signals from the bacterial microbiota have been shown to elicit a steady-state type I IFN response in systemic tissues and cell types that can prime antiviral immunity by several independent studies (Abt et al., 2012; Bradley et al., 2019; Ganal et al., 2012; Steed et al., 2017; Stefan et al., 2020; Winkler et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: A steady-state ISG signal has been observed in the intestine of uninfected mice.
source: Additionally, a steady-state ISG signal has been observed in the intestine of uninfected mice (Baldridge et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2016; Stockinger et al., 2014), but this intestinal response remained poorly characterized.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The hallmark gene set that was most enriched in IFN-λ-treated WT mice compared to unstimulated WT mice was INTERFERON_ALPHA_RESPONSE.
source: The hallmark gene set that was most enriched in IFN-λ-treated WT mice compared to unstimulated WT mice was INTERFERON_ALPHA_RESPONSE (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: INTERFERON_ALPHA_RESPONSE gene set reflects differences in IFN-λ responses between experimental conditions.
source: Therefore, this gene set reflects differences in IFN-λ responses between experimental conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that INTERFERON_ALPHA_RESPONSE was most enriched in IFN-λ-treated mice.

claim: ABX treatment reduced bacterial 16S gene copies in stool to below the limit of detection.
source: To deplete bacterial microbiota, we administered a cocktail of broad-spectrum ABX, and demonstrated that this treatment reduced bacterial 16S gene copies in stool to below the limit of detection (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: GSEA of WT mice treated with ABX showed a significant depletion of INTERFERON_ALPHA_RESPONSE hallmark genes in the ileum relative to WT mice with conventional microbiota.
source: GSEA of WT mice treated with ABX showed a significant depletion (negative enrichment score) of INTERFERON_ALPHA_RESPONSE hallmark genes in the ileum relative to WT mice with conventional microbiota (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ISGs are present at steady state in the ileum of specific-pathogen-free mice with conventional microbiota.
source: These data indicate that ISGs are present at steady state in the ileum of specific-pathogen-free mice with conventional microbiota
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ABX treatment depletes ISGs.

claim: Microbiota stimulate expression of ISGs in the ileum at homeostasis.
source: These data indicate that ISGs are present at steady state in the ileum of specific-pathogen-free mice with conventional microbiota and suggest that microbiota stimulate expression of these genes in the ileum at homeostasis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ABX treatment depletes ISGs.

claim: GSEA showed significant reduction of INTERFERON_ALPHA_RESPONSE hallmark genes in the ileum of Ifnlr1-/- mice compared to WT mice.
source: Indeed, GSEA showed significant reduction of INTERFERON_ALPHA_RESPONSE hallmark genes in the ileum of Ifnlr1-/- mice compared to WT mice (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Expression of INTERFERON_ALPHA_RESPONSE hallmark genes was not significantly decreased in Ifnlr1-/- mice treated with ABX compared to Ifnlr1-/- mice with conventional microbiota.
source: Furthermore, expression of INTERFERON_ALPHA_RESPONSE hallmark genes was not significantly decreased in Ifnlr1-/- mice treated with ABX compared to Ifnlr1-/- mice with conventional microbiota (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: INFLAMMATORY_RESPONSE and IL6_JAK_STAT3_SIGNALING hallmark gene sets were significantly decreased by ABX treatment in both WT mice and Ifnlr1-/- mice.
source: In contrast to INTERFERON_ALPHA_RESPONSE, other hallmark gene sets such as INFLAMMATORY_RESPONSE and IL6_JAK_STAT3_SIGNALING were significantly decreased by ABX treatment in both WT mice and Ifnlr1-/- mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ifnlr1 is necessary for the bacterial microbiota-dependent expression of ISGs in the ileum at homeostasis.
source: Together, these findings suggest that Ifnlr1 is necessary for the bacterial microbiota-dependent expression of ISGs in the ileum at homeostasis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ISGs are reduced in Ifnlr1-/- mice and not further reduced by ABX treatment.

claim: The bacterial microbiota stimulates IFN-λ responses in the ileum at homeostasis.
source: Since ISGs are enriched in mice upon IFN-λ stimulation and are decreased in Ifnlr1-/- and ABX-treated mice, we conclude that the bacterial microbiota stimulates IFN-λ responses in the ileum at homeostasis.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The DEGs shared by IFN-λ stimulation, ABX treatment, and Ifnlr1 deletion comprised a set of 21 genes that are decreased upon treatment with ABX and loss of Ifnlr1, and are induced in response to IFN-λ.
source: The DEGs shared by each of these comparisons comprised a set of 21 genes that are decreased upon treatment with ABX and loss of Ifnlr1, and are induced in response to IFN-λ (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: WT mice treated with IFN-λ had higher expression of all homeostatic ISGs than untreated mice.
source: WT mice treated with IFN-λ had higher expression of all homeostatic ISGs than untreated mice
evidence: This is supported by heatmap data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: WT mice with a conventional microbiota had higher expression of homeostatic ISGs than Ifnlr1-/- mice and ABX-treated mice of both genotypes.
source: WT mice with a conventional microbiota had higher expression of homeostatic ISGs than Ifnlr1-/- mice and ABX-treated mice of both genotypes (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by heatmap data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: ABX-treated Ifnlr1-/- mice do not show additional decreases in homeostatic ISGs relative to conventional Ifnlr1-/- mice.
source: We did not detect additional decreases in these homeostatic ISGs in ABX-treated Ifnlr1-/- mice relative to conventional Ifnlr1-/- mice, suggesting that Ifnlr1 is necessary for expression of homeostatic ISGs (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by heatmap data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Ifnlr1 is necessary for expression of homeostatic ISGs.
source: We did not detect additional decreases in these homeostatic ISGs in ABX-treated Ifnlr1-/- mice relative to conventional Ifnlr1-/- mice, suggesting that Ifnlr1 is necessary for expression of homeostatic ISGs (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ABX does not further reduce ISGs in Ifnlr1-/- mice.

claim: Homeostatic ISGs in both the ileum and colon are dependent on Ifnlr1 and the bacterial microbiota.
source: These data indicate that homeostatic ISGs in both the ileum and colon were dependent on Ifnlr1 and the bacterial microbiota
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Homeostatic ISGs are more abundantly expressed in ileal tissue than colonic tissue.
source: however, these homeostatic ISGs were more abundantly expressed in ileal tissue than colonic tissue (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Stimulation with small amounts of IFN-λ rescued ISG expression in whole tissue of ABX-treated mice.
source: Stimulation with small amounts of IFN-λ rescued ISG expression in whole tissue (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that that reduction of homeostatic ISG expression upon treatment with ABX is not due to an inability of the intestine to respond to IFN-λ.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The reduction of homeostatic ISG expression upon treatment with ABX is not due to an inability of the intestine to respond to IFN-λ.
source: Stimulation with small amounts of IFN-λ rescued ISG expression in whole tissue (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that that reduction of homeostatic ISG expression upon treatment with ABX is not due to an inability of the intestine to respond to IFN-λ.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that IFN-λ can rescue ISG expression in ABX-treated mice.

claim: ABX treatment and Ifnlr1 deletion did not reduce ISGs in MLN and spleen tissues.
source: We quantified Ifit1, Stat1, and Oas1a expression in the MLN and the spleen and found that ABX treatment and Ifnlr1 deletion did not reduce ISGs in these tissues (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Homeostatic ISGs include genes beyond the core signature identified in Figure 1.
source: Cumulatively, these data indicate that homeostatic ISGs include genes beyond the core signature identified in Figure 1 (e.g. Oas1a)
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Oas1a shows similar patterns to core ISGs but was not in the 21-gene set.

claim: Homeostatic ISGs are present in colonic tissue.
source: Cumulatively, these data indicate that homeostatic ISGs include genes beyond the core signature identified in Figure 1 (e.g. Oas1a), that homeostatic ISGs are present in colonic tissue
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Homeostatic IFN-λ-stimulated genes are most prominent in enteric tissues.
source: Cumulatively, these data indicate that homeostatic ISGs include genes beyond the core signature identified in Figure 1 (e.g. Oas1a), that homeostatic ISGs are present in colonic tissue, and that homeostatic IFN-λ-stimulated genes are most prominent in enteric tissues.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ISGs are reduced in intestinal tissues but not in MLN or spleen.

claim: Ifit1 expression in the ileum and colon of Trif-/- mice was not significantly different than in WT mice.
source: Ifit1 expression in the ileum and colon of Trif-/- mice was not significantly different than in WT mice, and Ifit1 expression was reduced with ABX in Trif-/- mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Ifit1 expression was reduced with ABX in Trif-/- mice.
source: Ifit1 expression in the ileum and colon of Trif-/- mice was not significantly different than in WT mice, and Ifit1 expression was reduced with ABX in Trif-/- mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mice lacking Myd88 exhibited tissue-specific decreases in Ifit1 expression, with significant decreases in the ileum, but not in the colon, relative to WT mice.
source: However, we found that mice lacking Myd88 exhibited tissue-specific decreases in Ifit1 expression, with significant decreases in the ileum, but not in the colon, relative to WT mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Signaling through MYD88, but not TRIF, is necessary for homeostatic ISG expression in the ileum.
source: These data are consistent with a previous report (Stockinger et al., 2014) and suggest that signaling through MYD88, but not TRIF, is necessary for homeostatic ISG expression in the ileum, whereas other factors may dominate in the colon.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Myd88-/- but not Trif-/- mice show reduced ISGs in the ileum.

claim: IRF3 is not required for homeostatic IFN-λ induction.
source: We did not observe significant decreases in Ifit1 expression in the ileum or the colon of Irf3-/- mice as compared to WT (Figure 3B), indicating that IRF3 is not required for homeostatic IFN-λ induction.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Ifit1 expression in both the ileum and colon of Irf7-/- mice was modestly (twofold) decreased compared to WT mice.
source: However, we observed a modest (twofold) decrease in Ifit1 expression in both the ileum and colon of Irf7-/- mice when compared to WT mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: IRF7 is not necessary for the homeostatic ISG response to the bacterial microbiota.
source: Although IRF7 is implicated by these data, it does not appear to be strictly required for homeostatic expression of Ifit1 because expression is further reduced by ABX treatment (Figure 3B). These data suggest that IRF7 is not necessary for the homeostatic ISG response to the bacterial microbiota.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ABX further reduces ISGs in Irf7-/- mice.

claim: Ifit1 expression was not significantly different in either ileum or colon tissue of Ifnar1-/- mice compared to WT.
source: Ifit1 expression was not significantly different in either ileum or colon tissue of Ifnar1-/- mice compared to WT (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Ifit1 expression was significantly lower in ileum and colon tissue of Stat1-/- mice compared to Ifnar1-/- and WT mice.
source: However, Ifit1 expression was significantly lower in ileum and colon tissue of Stat1-/- mice compared to Ifnar1-/- and WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Treatment of Stat1-/- mice with ABX did not further reduce Ifit1 expression.
source: Importantly, treatment of Stat1-/- mice with ABX did not further reduce Ifit1 expression, emphasizing the necessity of STAT1 for this homeostatic ISG response.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: STAT1 is necessary for the homeostatic ISG response.
source: Importantly, treatment of Stat1-/- mice with ABX did not further reduce Ifit1 expression, emphasizing the necessity of STAT1 for this homeostatic ISG response.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ABX does not further reduce ISGs in Stat1-/- mice.

claim: Ifit1 expression was not significantly different in Ifnlr1-/+/Ifnar1-/- relative to Ifnlr1-/+/Ifnar1-/+ controls in ileal tissue.
source: We found that Ifit1 expression was not significantly different in Ifnlr1-/+/Ifnar1-/- relative to Ifnlr1-/+/Ifnar1-/+ controls in ileal tissue (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Ifit1 expression in Ifnlr1-/-/Ifnar1-/+ was significantly lower compared to Ifnlr1-/+/Ifnar1-/+ controls, but was not significantly different from Ifnlr1-/-/Ifnar1-/- mice.
source: Ifit1 expression in Ifnlr1-/-/Ifnar1-/+ was significantly lower compared to Ifnlr1-/+/Ifnar1-/+ controls, but was not significantly different from Ifnlr1-/-/Ifnar1-/- mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Homeostatic ISG expression in the intestine is partly dependent on MYD88, and is independent of type I IFN signaling.
source: Cumulatively, these data indicate that homeostatic ISG expression in the intestine is partly dependent on MYD88, and is independent of type I IFN signaling.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from multiple experiments with knockout mice.

claim: Treatment with ABX or loss of Ifnlr1 reduced homeostatic ISGs in the IEC fraction.
source: Treatment with ABX or loss of Ifnlr1 reduced homeostatic ISGs in the IEC fraction, but the lamina propria had low expression of these ISGs relative to the epithelium of untreated WT mice, regardless of treatment or genotype (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from fractionated tissue shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The lamina propria had low expression of homeostatic ISGs relative to the epithelium of untreated WT mice, regardless of treatment or genotype.
source: Treatment with ABX or loss of Ifnlr1 reduced homeostatic ISGs in the IEC fraction, but the lamina propria had low expression of these ISGs relative to the epithelium of untreated WT mice, regardless of treatment or genotype (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from fractionated tissue shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Conditional deletion of Ifnlr1 in IECs reduced Ifit1 and Oas1a to a similar extent as the reduction observed in Ifnlr1-/- animals.
source: Conditional deletion of Ifnlr1 in IECs reduced Ifit1 and Oas1a to a similar extent as the reduction observed in Ifnlr1-/- animals, above (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Homeostatic ISGs are dependent on Ifnlr1 expression by IECs.
source: Together, these findings indicate that homeostatic ISGs are dependent on Ifnlr1 expression by IECs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that conditional deletion of Ifnlr1 in IECs reduces ISGs.

claim: CD45+ cells from the intestinal epithelial and lamina propria fraction expressed detectable Ifnl2/3 at homeostasis, but EpCAM+ cells did not.
source: We found that CD45+ cells from the intestinal epithelial and lamina propria fraction expressed detectable Ifnl2/3 at homeostasis, but EpCAM+ cells did not, which is consistent with Mahlakõiv et al.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from enriched cell populations shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Expression of Ifnl2/3 in CD45+ cells from the epithelial fraction was significantly reduced with ABX treatment.
source: Furthermore, we found that expression of Ifnl2/3 in CD45+ cells from the epithelial fraction was significantly reduced with ABX treatment
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CD45+ cells from lamina propria had a non-statistically significant (p = 0.0523) reduction in Ifnl2/3 expression with ABX treatment.
source: and CD45+ cells from lamina propria had a non-statistically significant (p = 0.0523) reduction in Ifnl2/3 expression with ABX treatment (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Epithelium-associated CD45+ leukocytes are the likely source of homeostatic IFN-λ in response to bacterial microbiota.
source: From these data, we conclude that epithelium-associated CD45+ leukocytes are the likely source of homeostatic IFN-λ in response to bacterial microbiota, but we do not rule out additional involvement of CD45+ cells in the lamina propria.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CD45+ cells in the epithelial fraction express Ifnl2/3 in a microbiota-dependent manner.

claim: CD45+ cells of the epithelial fraction modestly expressed IFN-β transcript (Ifnb1) at homeostasis.
source: Similar to Ifnl2/3, we found that CD45+ cells of the epithelial fraction modestly expressed IFN-β transcript (Ifnb1) at homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: CD45+ cells of the lamina propria robustly expressed Ifnb1 at homeostasis.
source: Additionally, CD45+ cells of the lamina propria robustly expressed Ifnb1 at homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Ifnb1 was not decreased in mice treated with ABX.
source: However, unlike Ifnl2/3, Ifnb1 was not decreased in mice treated with ABX (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Ifnb1 expression by CD45+ cells in the intestine is less dependent on stimulation by bacterial microbiota relative to Ifnl2/3.
source: These data indicate that Ifnb1 expression by CD45+ cells in the intestine is less dependent on stimulation by bacterial microbiota relative to Ifnl2/3, consistent with the dominant role of IFN-λ responses in driving homeostatic ISG expression in the epithelium.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Ifnb1 is not reduced by ABX treatment while Ifnl2/3 is.

claim: RNAscope staining of the ileum from untreated WT mice revealed localized pockets of robust Ifit1 expression in individual villi rather than ubiquitously low expression throughout the intestinal epithelium.
source: Contrary to our hypothesis, RNAscope staining of the ileum from untreated WT mice revealed localized pockets of robust Ifit1 expression in individual villi rather than ubiquitously low expression throughout the intestinal epithelium (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Ifit1 localization was skewed away from the crypt and toward the tips of individual villi within the ileum.
source: Additionally, Ifit1 localization was skewed away from the crypt and toward the tips of individual villi within the ileum
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The distinct ISG Usp18 co-localized with Ifit1.
source: and this localization was not specific to Ifit1 because the distinct ISG Usp18 co-localized with Ifit1 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope imaging data showing co-localization in Figure 6A.

claim: Homeostatic ISGs are sporadically expressed in individual villi and are primarily localized to mature enterocytes that are most distally located in villi.
source: These data indicate that homeostatic ISGs are sporadically expressed in individual villi and are primarily localized to mature enterocytes that are most distally located in villi.
evidence: This is inferred from the imaging data showing localized expression toward villus tips.

claim: Localized ISG expression within individual villi was not due to a localized ability to respond to IFN-λ because stimulation with exogenous IFN-λ resulted in Ifit1 expression within all intestinal villi, but not intestinal crypts.
source: We determined that localized ISG expression within individual villi was not due to a localized ability to respond to IFN-λ because stimulation with exogenous IFN-λ resulted in Ifit1 expression within all intestinal villi, but not intestinal crypts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope imaging data after IFN-λ treatment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The minimal expression of Ifit1 within intestinal crypts following exogenous IFN-λ treatment suggests that homeostatic ISGs are localized to mature enterocytes because intestinal crypts do not exhibit robust responses to IFN-λ.
source: The minimal expression of Ifit1 within intestinal crypts following exogenous IFN-λ treatment suggests that homeostatic ISGs are localized to mature enterocytes because intestinal crypts do not exhibit robust responses to IFN-λ.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that crypts lack Ifit1 expression even after IFN-λ treatment.

claim: The non-uniform distribution of homeostatic Ifit1 expression was ablated in the ileum of mice treated with ABX.
source: Additionally, the non-uniform distribution of homeostatic Ifit1 expression was ablated in the ileum of mice treated with ABX (Figure 6B–D), consistent with a dependency on bacterial microbiota.
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope imaging data shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: The localized Ifit1 expression observed in untreated WT mice was recapitulated in Ifnlr1flox/flox mice.
source: We found that the localized Ifit1 expression observed in untreated WT mice was recapitulated in Ifnlr1flox/flox mice (Figure 6E)
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope imaging data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Areas of ISG expression were ablated in Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO mice.
source: but these areas of ISG expression were ablated in Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO mice (Figure 6F–G).
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope imaging data shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: Localized Ifit1 staining is also observed in the colonic epithelium.
source: Lastly, we found that this discrete localization of the homeostatic ISG response is not limited to the ileum, as localized Ifit1 staining is also observed in the colonic epithelium (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Homeostatic ISGs are expressed in a highly localized manner within the intestinal epithelium.
source: Together, our analyses indicated that homeostatic ISGs are expressed in a highly localized manner within the intestinal epithelium.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from imaging data showing localized ISG expression.

claim: Homeostatic ISGs were predominantly expressed in mature enterocyte subtypes in the Haber et al. mouse scRNA-seq dataset.
source: Homeostatic ISGs were predominantly expressed in mature enterocyte subtypes, which clustered separately from crypt-resident progenitor IECs such as transit amplifying (TA) cells and stem cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A significantly higher percentage of enterocytes express homeostatic ISGs than crypt-associated cells in the Haber et al. mouse scRNA-seq dataset.
source: We found that a significantly higher percentage of enterocytes express homeostatic ISGs than crypt-associated cells, but that these homeostatic ISGs were expressed in a relatively small proportion of enterocytes (<20%) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Homeostatic ISGs were expressed in a relatively small proportion of enterocytes (<20%) in the Haber et al. mouse scRNA-seq dataset.
source: We found that a significantly higher percentage of enterocytes express homeostatic ISGs than crypt-associated cells, but that these homeostatic ISGs were expressed in a relatively small proportion of enterocytes (<20%) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Ifit1 was present in ~5% of enterocytes by scRNA-seq in the Haber et al. dataset.
source: Notably, Ifit1 (highlighted in red) was present in ~5% of enterocytes by scRNA-seq, which is consistent with our observation of 1–4% Ifit1-positive area by imaging the mouse small intestine (Figure 6B–G).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The relative absence of ISG-positive crypt-associated cells in the Haber et al. scRNA-seq data is consistent with the observation that intestinal crypts lacked Ifit1 and Usp18 expression by imaging.
source: Furthermore, the relative absence of ISG-positive crypt-associated cells in this scRNA-seq data is consistent with our observation that intestinal crypts lacked Ifit1 and Usp18 expression by imaging.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of scRNA-seq data with imaging data.

claim: Homeostatic ISGs were present in significantly more enterocytes than crypt-associated cells in the Elmentaite et al. human scRNA-seq dataset.
source: Similar to mice, homeostatic ISGs were present in significantly more enterocytes than crypt-associated cells, and most homeostatic ISGs in this human dataset were present in a relatively small proportion of cells (<20%).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of human scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Most homeostatic ISGs in the Elmentaite et al. human dataset were present in a relatively small proportion of cells (<20%).
source: Similar to mice, homeostatic ISGs were present in significantly more enterocytes than crypt-associated cells, and most homeostatic ISGs in this human dataset were present in a relatively small proportion of cells (<20%).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of human scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: ISGs may be present in a small proportion of IECs from healthy, human ileal tissue at homeostasis.
source: These human data suggest that ISGs may be present in a small proportion of IECs from healthy, human ileal tissue at homeostasis and may share the localization observed in our murine analyses.
evidence: This is inferred from analysis of human scRNA-seq data.

claim: Homeostatic ISGs are not ubiquitously expressed throughout the intestinal epithelium; rather, they are expressed in a minority of IECs and skewed toward mature enterocytes along the crypt-villus axis.
source: Our analysis of a murine scRNA-seq dataset support our previous observations that homeostatic ISGs are not ubiquitously expressed throughout the intestinal epithelium; rather, they are expressed in a minority of IECs and skewed toward mature enterocytes along the crypt-villus axis.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from analysis of scRNA-seq data.

claim: Localized Ifit1 expression was visible in 4/12 ABX-treated Ifnlr1flox/flox mice administered LPS.
source: However, localized Ifit1 expression was visible in 4/12 ABX-treated Ifnlr1flox/flox mice administered LPS (Figure 8E and H–I).
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope imaging data shown in Figure 8E and quantification in Figure 8H-I.

claim: In ABX-treated Ifnlr1flox/flox mice treated with fecal transplant of conventional microbes, localized expression of Ifit1 was visible in 4/8 mice.
source: In ABX-treated Ifnlr1flox/flox mice treated with fecal transplant of conventional microbes, localized expression of Ifit1 was visible in 4/8 mice (Figure 8F and H–I).
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope imaging data shown in Figure 8F and quantification in Figure 8H-I.

claim: Localized Ifit1 expression was not observed in Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO mice following LPS administration.
source: Importantly, we did not observe localized Ifit1 expression in Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO mice following LPS administration (Figure 8G), indicating that LPS-stimulated Ifit1 depends on IEC expression of Ifnlr1.
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope imaging data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: LPS-stimulated Ifit1 depends on IEC expression of Ifnlr1.
source: Importantly, we did not observe localized Ifit1 expression in Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO mice following LPS administration (Figure 8G), indicating that LPS-stimulated Ifit1 depends on IEC expression of Ifnlr1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that LPS does not induce Ifit1 in Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO mice.

claim: LPS administration non-significantly increased (p = 0.1022) the proportion of mice that were Ifit1-positive.
source: Statistical analysis by Fisher's exact test indicated that LPS administration non-significantly increased (p = 0.1022) the proportion of mice that were Ifit1-positive
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 8J.

claim: Fecal reconstitution of ABX-treated mice significantly increased the likelihood of these mice being Ifit1-positive.
source: whereas fecal reconstitution of ABX-treated mice significantly increased the likelihood of these mice being Ifit1-positive (Figure 8J).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 8J.

claim: Mice that received fecal transplant had full restoration of 16S gene copies despite only 4/8 having homeostatic Ifit1 expression.
source: Importantly, mice that received fecal transplant had full restoration of 16S gene copies (Figure 8K) despite only 4/8 having homeostatic Ifit1 expression.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8K.

claim: Reconstitution of the homeostatic ISG signal by fecal transfer has incomplete penetrance at this timepoint.
source: These findings suggest that reconstitution of the homeostatic ISG signal by fecal transfer has incomplete penetrance at this timepoint, underscoring the incomplete presence of localized Ifit1 expression (4/12) in ABX-treated mice administered peroral LPS.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that bacterial reconstitution does not always restore ISG expression.

claim: Peroral administration of LPS to ABX-treated mice increased the proportion of ISG-positive tissues by 21–36%.
source: However, stratification of tissues into positive and negative for each ISG indicated that peroral administration of LPS to ABX-treated mice increased the proportion of ISG-positive tissues by 21–36% (Ifit1: p = 0.065; Stat1, p < 0.05; Oas1a, p < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Peroral administration of flagellin significantly increased the proportion of ISG-positive mice by 25–44%.
source: Additionally, peroral administration of flagellin significantly increased the proportion of ISG-positive mice by 25–44% (Ifit1: p = 0.052; Stat1, p < 0.01; Oas1a, p < 0.05)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: CpG DNA did not significantly increase the proportion of ISG-positive mice.
source: whereas CpG DNA did not significantly increase the proportion of ISG-positive mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: LPS and flagellin are sufficient to stimulate homeostatic ISG expression in a significant proportion of ABX-treated mice.
source: Together, these data suggest that LPS and flagellin are sufficient to stimulate homeostatic ISG expression in a significant proportion of ABX-treated mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that LPS and flagellin increase ISG-positive mice.

claim: The ability of multiple PRR ligands to stimulate homeostatic ISGs suggests that exposure to a variety of bacterial MAMPs is the basis for localized, homeostatic ISG expression.
source: The ability of multiple PRR ligands to stimulate homeostatic ISGs suggests that exposure to a variety of bacterial MAMPs is the basis for localized, homeostatic ISG expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that multiple bacterial components can stimulate ISGs.

claim: Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO mice shed 20-fold more mRV genomes into their stool than Ifnlr1flox/flox mice at day 2 after inoculation.
source: We first detected mRV shedding in the stool on day 2 after inoculation and, at this early timepoint, Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO mice shed 20-fold more mRV genomes into their stool than Ifnlr1flox/flox mice (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from stool shown in Figure 9A.

claim: At the peak of viral shedding between days 3 and 5, there were no significant differences between Ifnlr1flox/flox and Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO littermates.
source: However, at the peak of viral shedding between days 3 and 5, there were no significant differences between Ifnlr1flox/flox and Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO littermates (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from stool shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The similarity at peak of viral shedding was consistent with an ability of mRV to evade the host IFN response once infection is established.
source: This similarity at peak of viral shedding was consistent with an ability of mRV to evade the host IFN response once infection is established.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that differences in shedding are only seen early in infection.

claim: Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO mice have defects in protection against initiation of mRV infection.
source: Together, these findings suggest that Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO mice have defects in protection against initiation of mRV infection and that the protective capacity of endogenous IFN-λ signaling against mRV is primarily prophylactic in nature.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that differences in infection are only seen at early timepoints.

claim: The protective capacity of endogenous IFN-λ signaling against mRV is primarily prophylactic in nature.
source: Together, these findings suggest that Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO mice have defects in protection against initiation of mRV infection and that the protective capacity of endogenous IFN-λ signaling against mRV is primarily prophylactic in nature.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that protection is only seen at early timepoints.

claim: At 24 hr post-inoculation, Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO mice had 20-fold more mRV genomes than Ifnlr1flox/flox mice.
source: At 24 hr post-inoculation, we found that Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO mice had 20-fold more mRV genomes than Ifnlr1flox/flox mice (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: A threefold greater proportion of IECs were infected with mRV in Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO mice than Ifnlr1flox/flox mice at 24 hr post-infection.
source: In addition, we found that a threefold greater proportion of IECs were infected with mRV in Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO mice than Ifnlr1flox/flox mice at 24 hr post-infection (Figure 9C–F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 9C-F.

claim: The median fluorescence intensity (MFI) of mRV antigen was equivalent in mRV-infected IECs from Ifnlr1flox/flox and Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO mice.
source: However, the median fluorescence intensity (MFI) of mRV antigen was equivalent in mRV-infected IECs from Ifnlr1flox/flox and Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO mice (Figure 9G)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 9G.

claim: The MFI of mRV did not correlate (r2 = 0.0003) with the percentage of infected IECs.
source: and the MFI of mRV did not correlate (r2 = 0.0003) with the percentage of infected IECs (Figure 9H).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 9H.

claim: The protective role of Ifnlr1 is to prevent infection of IECs rather than to limit replication within IECs after they are infected.
source: This equivalent mRV antigen burden in infected cells from Ifnlr1flox/flox and Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO mice in combination with the lack of correlation between antigen burden and percentage of infected cells suggests that the protective role of Ifnlr1 is to prevent infection of IECs rather than to limit replication within IECs after they are infected.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that MFI is equivalent but percentage of infected cells differs.

claim: The 12 and 24 hr timepoints capture the earliest detectable infection of IECs by mRV.
source: Thus, the 12 and 24 hr timepoints capture the earliest detectable infection of IECs by mRV, and this early infection is significantly reduced by IFN-λ signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that infection is near the limit of detection at 12 hr.

claim: Early infection of IECs by mRV is significantly reduced by IFN-λ signaling.
source: Thus, the 12 and 24 hr timepoints capture the earliest detectable infection of IECs by mRV, and this early infection is significantly reduced by IFN-λ signaling.
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced infection in Ifnlr1-sufficient mice at early timepoints.

claim: A minority (~30%) of mRV-infected cells were Ifit1+ at 12 or 24 hr post-inoculation.
source: Quantification of co-staining for Ifit1 in mRV-infected cells indicated that a minority (~30%) were Ifit1+ at 12 or 24 hr post-inoculation
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope imaging data shown in Figure 9I-J.

claim: A majority (~63%) of mRV-infected cells were Ifit1+ at 96 hr post-inoculation.
source: whereas a majority (~63%) of mRV-infected cells were Ifit1+ at 96 hr post-inoculation (Figure 9I–J, Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope imaging data shown in Figure 9I-J.

claim: Co-staining data are consistent with early mRV evasion of IFN responses within infected IECs at the same timepoints that increased infection of Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO mice was observed.
source: These co-staining data are consistent with early mRV evasion of IFN responses within infected IECs at the same timepoints that we observed increased infection of Ifnlr1 IEC-cKO mice (Figure 9B–F, Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most infected cells are Ifit1-negative at early timepoints.

claim: mRV inoculation did not increase the area of Ifit1 expression in the intestine at 12–24 hr post-inoculation.
source: Furthermore, we found mRV inoculation did not increase the area of Ifit1 expression in the intestine at 12–24 hr post-inoculation.
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope imaging data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 3.

claim: At 96 hr post-inoculation, there was a significant increase in epithelial Ifit1 expression in the ileum that coincided with increased viral genomes and antigen.
source: However, at 96 hr post-inoculation, we found a significant increase in epithelial Ifit1 expression in the ileum that coincided with increased viral genomes and antigen (Figure 9—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope imaging and qPCR data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 3.

claim: Ifit1 expression at 12 and 24 hr post-inoculation is primarily due to the preexisting homeostatic response rather than in response to mRV infection.
source: suggesting that Ifit1 expression at 12 and 24 hr post-inoculation is primarily due to the preexisting homeostatic response rather than in response to mRV infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Ifit1 area does not increase at early timepoints after infection.

claim: Homeostatic ISGs stimulated by Ifnlr1 expression on IECs play an early protective role against viral infection that preempts viral IFN evasion mechanisms.
source: Therefore, we propose that homeostatic ISGs stimulated by Ifnlr1 expression on IECs play an early protective role against viral infection that preempts viral IFN evasion mechanisms.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Bacterial microbiota induce an enteric IFN-λ response in IECs at homeostasis.
source: Here, we report that bacterial microbiota induce an enteric IFN-λ response in IECs at homeostasis (Figures 1—4).
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experiments.

claim: The homeostatic response is dependent on the IFN-λ receptor.
source: Although there are previous reports of basal, non-receptor-dependent ISG expression in immortalized and primary cell lines (Hakim et al., 2018), the homeostatic response that we report here is dependent on the IFN-λ receptor.
evidence: This is supported by data showing loss of ISGs in Ifnlr1-/- mice.

claim: The homeostatic ISG response is independent of type I IFN signaling.
source: Furthermore, we find this response is independent of type I IFN signaling (Figure 3), indicating that IFN-λ signaling plays a dominant and active role in the gastrointestinal epithelium.
evidence: This is supported by data showing no reduction of ISGs in Ifnar1-/- mice.

claim: IFN-λ signaling plays a dominant and active role in the gastrointestinal epithelium.
source: Furthermore, we find this response is independent of type I IFN signaling (Figure 3), indicating that IFN-λ signaling plays a dominant and active role in the gastrointestinal epithelium.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that homeostatic ISGs are independent of type I IFN.

claim: Minimal changes in ISG expression were found within the spleen and MLN after ABX treatment.
source: We also find minimal changes in ISG expression within the spleen and MLN after ABX treatment, suggesting that homeostatic ISGs are predominantly expressed in the intestine.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Homeostatic ISGs are predominantly expressed in the intestine.
source: We also find minimal changes in ISG expression within the spleen and MLN after ABX treatment, suggesting that homeostatic ISGs are predominantly expressed in the intestine.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ISGs are not reduced in spleen and MLN by ABX treatment.

claim: Homeostatic ISGs are substantially present in IECs.
source: Therefore, we conclude that homeostatic ISGs are substantially present in IECs, but do not dispute the prior findings that relatively low homeostatic ISG expression induced by type I IFN plays an important role in extra-intestinal tissues and non-epithelial cell types.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from fractionation experiments.

claim: Homeostatic expression of Ifnl2/3 is dependent on bacterial microbiota.
source: We have confirmed these findings and have extended them to show that this homeostatic expression of Ifnl2/3, but not Ifnb1, is dependent on bacterial microbiota (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The production of IFN-λ is below the limit of detection by imaging or highly transient in nature.
source: However, we have been unable to detect IFN-λ transcripts by RNA scope in situ hybridization in mice at homeostasis, consistent with recently published data (Ingle et al., 2021). This suggests that the production of IFN-λ is below the limit of detection by imaging or highly transient in nature.
evidence: This is inferred from the inability to detect IFN-λ by imaging.

claim: Proximity to bacterial stimuli may be a primary determinant in homeostatic IFN-λ production.
source: Although the cell type that produces homeostatic IFN-λ is unknown, enrichment for Ifnl2/3 in CD45+ cells within the intestinal epithelial fraction suggests that proximity to bacterial stimuli may be a primary determinant in this response.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CD45+ cells in the epithelial fraction express Ifnl2/3.

claim: CD45+ cells may be actively surveying the intestinal epithelium to detect bacterial MAMPs.
source: We suggest that these cells may be actively surveying the intestinal epithelium to detect bacterial MAMPs.
evidence: This is speculation based on the localization of Ifnl2/3-expressing cells.

claim: Localized ISG expression may reflect the distribution of cells capable of sensing bacterial microbiota, distinct microenvironments within the gastrointestinal tract, or qualitative differences in bacterial colonization.
source: The basis for localized ISG expression is unknown; however, it may reflect the distribution of cells capable of sensing bacterial microbiota, distinct microenvironments within the gastrointestinal tract, or qualitative differences in bacterial colonization.
evidence: This is speculation about the basis for localized ISG expression.

claim: The bacterial microbiota broadly stimulates homeostatic IFN-λ through multiple, redundant PRRs.
source: These data suggest that the bacterial microbiota broadly stimulates homeostatic IFN-λ through multiple, redundant PRRs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that multiple PRR ligands can stimulate ISGs and different PRRs are required in different tissues.

claim: Localization is an intrinsic property of homeostatic ISG stimulation and is not likely to be due to qualitative differences in bacterial colonization.
source: Furthermore, the presence of localized Ifit1 expression in ABX-treated mice following LPS administration (Figure 8) suggests that localization is an intrinsic property of homeostatic ISG stimulation and is not likely to be due to qualitative differences in bacterial colonization.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that LPS can induce localized ISG expression in ABX-treated mice.

claim: ISG localization may be indicative of regional differences in access of luminal bacterial MAMPs to IFN-λ-producing cells.
source: ISG localization may be indicative of regional differences in access of luminal bacterial MAMPs to IFN-λ-producing cells.
evidence: This is speculation about the basis for ISG localization.

claim: The signature of homeostatic ISGs in ileum tissue included well-characterized antiviral ISGs.
source: Although bacterial-associated, IFN-independent mechanisms of mRV clearance have been reported (Shi et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2014), we found that the signature of homeostatic ISGs in ileum tissue included well-characterized antiviral ISGs (Figures 1–2).
evidence: This is supported by the identification of ISGs like Ifit1 in the homeostatic signature.

claim: Protection offered by IEC expression of Ifnlr1 was lost by the middle and late stages of mRV infection.
source: However, the protection offered by IEC expression of Ifnlr1 was lost by the middle and late stages of infection, consistent with the ability of mRV to antagonize induction of IFN responses once infection is established (Arnold et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by data showing no difference in viral shedding at later timepoints.

claim: Prophylactic administration of exogenous IFN-λ protects against mRV infection.
source: Ultimately, it is clear that prophylactic administration of exogenous IFN-λ protects against mRV infection (Lin et al., 2016; Pott et al., 2011; Van Winkle et al., 2020), providing precedent that homeostatic IFN-λ would also be protective when induced by bacterial microbiota prior to infection.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Localized ISGs may be indicative of locations that are particularly vulnerable to viral infection if ISGs were not present at the time of viral exposure.
source: Given our findings in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1, we suggest that these localized ISGs may be indicative of locations that are particularly vulnerable to viral infection if ISGs were not present at the time of viral exposure.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of localized ISGs.

claim: Preexisting, homeostatic ISGs present in Ifnlr1-sufficient mice are protective during initiation of mRV infection.
source: In sum, these findings indicate that preexisting, homeostatic ISGs present in Ifnlr1-sufficient mice are protective during initiation of mRV infection, but that endogenous IFN-λ does not reduce mRV burden in infected cells.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from mRV infection experiments.

claim: Endogenous IFN-λ does not reduce mRV burden in infected cells.
source: In sum, these findings indicate that preexisting, homeostatic ISGs present in Ifnlr1-sufficient mice are protective during initiation of mRV infection, but that endogenous IFN-λ does not reduce mRV burden in infected cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that MFI of mRV is equivalent in infected cells from both genotypes.

claim: Detection of bacterial microbiota in particularly exposed areas may preemptively activate homeostatic ISGs as a form of anticipatory immunity to protect the intestinal epithelium from enteric viruses.
source: These data highlight the possibility that detection of bacterial microbiota in particularly exposed areas may preemptively activate homeostatic ISGs as a form of anticipatory immunity to protect the intestinal epithelium from enteric viruses.
evidence: This is the main conclusion and interpretation of the study.
